p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming led his army to Mian County. Passing Ma Chao's grave, he ordered Ma Chao's younger brother Ma Dai to put on mourning and personally offered sacrifice at the tomb. When the rites were over, he returned to camp to discuss the advance. Suddenly a scout reported, “The Wei emperor Cao Rui has sent his son-in-law Xiahou Mao to muster troops from every command in Guanzhong and come against us.” Wei Yan came before the command tent and proposed a plan: “Xiahou Mao is a pampered son of privilege, timid and without strategy. Give me five thousand picked men. I shall take the road through Baozhong, follow the Qinling eastward, then turn north through Ziwu Valley; within ten days I can reach Chang'an. If Xiahou Mao hears of my sudden arrival, he will surely abandon the city and flee toward the granaries by Hengmen. While I advance from the east, Chancellor, you may drive the main army forward through Xie Valley. Thus all the land west of Xianyang may be settled in a single stroke.” Kongming laughed. “That is no perfectly secure plan. You presume the Central Plains has no capable men. Should someone advise placing troops in the mountain defiles to cut you off and destroy you, not only would your five thousand men perish, but our fighting spirit would suffer a grievous blow. It cannot possibly be adopted.” Wei Yan replied, “If the Chancellor advances by the main road, the enemy will surely raise every soldier in Guanzhong to meet us along the way. The campaign will drag on endlessly. When, then, shall we ever win the Central Plains?” Kongming said, “I shall proceed from Longyou by broad, level roads and advance according to proper methods. Why should I fear defeat?” And so he did not adopt Wei Yan's plan. Wei Yan withdrew, deeply displeased. Kongming sent a messenger ordering Zhao Yun to advance.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xiahou Mao was gathering troops from every quarter at Chang'an. At that time the Xiliang general Han De arrived with eighty thousand troops drawn from the Western Qiang commands. He wielded a great mountain-cleaving axe and possessed the valor to withstand ten thousand men. When he appeared before Xiahou Mao, Mao rewarded him lavishly and appointed him vanguard. Han De had four sons, all highly skilled in arms and exceptional with bow and horse: the eldest, Han Ying; the second, Han Yao; the third, Han Qiong; and the fourth, Han Qi. Han De took his four sons and eighty thousand Western Qiang troops by way of Mount Fengming, where they encountered the Shu army. The two armies drew up opposite one another. Han De rode forth, with his four sons arrayed on either side. Han De bellowed abuse: “Traitors to the realm! How dare you violate our borders!” Zhao Yun flew into a rage, leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and challenged Han De to single combat. Han Ying, the eldest son, galloped out to meet him. Before three bouts had passed, Zhao Yun thrust him dead beneath his horse with a single stroke of the spear. Seeing this, the second son, Han Yao, brandished his sword and charged on horseback. Zhao Yun displayed the tigerish might of former days, rallied his spirit, and met the attack. Han Yao could not withstand him. The third son, Han Qiong, hastily leveled his halberd, spurred forward, and joined the attack. Zhao Yun showed no fear, and his spearwork never faltered. When the fourth son, Han Qi, saw that his two brothers could not defeat Zhao Yun, he too galloped in, whirling a pair of sun-and-moon swords, and they surrounded Zhao Yun. At the center, Zhao Yun fought the three generals alone. Before long, Han Qi was struck by the spear and fell from his horse. A subordinate general from Han De's ranks rushed out and rescued him. Zhao Yun trailed his spear and fled. Han Qiong laid aside his halberd, hastily took up bow and arrows, and shot at him. He loosed three arrows in succession, but Zhao Yun knocked them all down with his spear. Enraged, Han Qiong seized his halberd again and galloped after him. But an arrow from Zhao Yun struck him squarely in the face, and he fell dead from his horse. Han Yao spurred forward, raised his precious blade, and hacked at Zhao Yun. Zhao Yun cast his spear to the ground, dodged the blade, captured Han Yao alive, and carried him back to his lines. Then he spurred out once more, recovered his spear, and charged through the enemy array. Seeing all four sons fall to Zhao Yun, Han De felt his heart and gall split with anguish and fled first into his own ranks. The Western Qiang troops had long known Zhao Yun's fame. Now that they saw his valor undiminished from former days, who dared cross weapons with him? Wherever Zhao Yun's horse went, rank after rank fell back. Alone on a single horse with a single spear, Zhao Yun charged back and forth as though entering an empty land. A later poet praised him in verse:

p.src: Seeing Zhao Yun's great victory, Deng Zhi led the Shu troops in a sweeping attack, and the Xiliang army fled in utter defeat. Han De narrowly escaped capture by Zhao Yun; casting off his armor, he fled on foot. Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi recalled their troops and returned to camp. Deng Zhi congratulated him: “General, though you have reached seventy years of age, your valor is as great as ever. Today you slew four generals before the lines—a feat rarely seen in this world!” Zhao Yun replied, “The Chancellor thought me too old and was unwilling to employ me. I merely wished to show what I could still do.” He then sent men to escort Han Yao away and deliver a written report of the victory to Kongming.

p.src: Meanwhile, Han De led his defeated troops back to Xiahou Mao and tearfully recounted what had happened. Xiahou Mao personally led his army out to meet Zhao Yun. A scout rode into the Shu camp and reported that Xiahou Mao was approaching with his army. Zhao Yun seized his spear, mounted, and led a little over a thousand men to form an array before Mount Fengming. That day Xiahou Mao wore a golden helmet, rode a white horse, and held a great cleaver as he stood beneath his command standard. Seeing Zhao Yun gallop back and forth with spear leveled, Xiahou Mao wished to fight him himself. Han De said, “How can I fail to avenge the enemy who slew my four sons?” Spurring his horse and swinging his mountain-cleaving axe, he charged straight at Zhao Yun. Zhao Yun furiously leveled his spear and met him. Before three bouts had passed, Zhao Yun thrust Han De dead beneath his horse, then wheeled swiftly and charged straight at Xiahou Mao. In alarm, Xiahou Mao darted back into his own ranks. Deng Zhi drove his troops forward in a sweeping assault. The Wei army suffered another defeat, withdrew over ten li, and made camp. That night Xiahou Mao gathered his generals and said, “I have long heard Zhao Yun's name, but never saw him face to face. Today he is old, yet his heroic power remains. Only now do I believe the tales of Changban at Dangyang. Since no one can match him, what are we to do?” The army adviser Cheng Wu, son of Cheng Yu, came forward and said, “By my judgment, Zhao Yun has courage but no strategy and need not trouble us. Tomorrow, Commander, lead the army out again, first concealing two forces to left and right. Before the lines, feign retreat and lure Zhao Yun to the ambush. Then climb the hill and direct the troops on every side to surround him in layer upon layer. Zhao Yun can then be captured.” Xiahou Mao accepted the proposal. He sent Dong Xi with thirty thousand men to lie in ambush on the left and Xue Ze with thirty thousand on the right. The two completed their preparations.

p.src: The next day Xiahou Mao once more marshaled drums, gongs, banners, and standards and led his army forward. Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi went out to meet him. From horseback Deng Zhi said to Zhao Yun, “The Wei army fled in great defeat last night, yet has returned today. There must be trickery. Old General, be on your guard.” Zilong replied, “What account need we take of this callow boy? Today I shall surely capture him!” He galloped forth. The Wei general Pan Sui came out to meet him, but before three bouts had passed, he wheeled his horse and fled. Zhao Yun pursued, and eight Wei generals came out together to meet him. They let Xiahou Mao escape first, then the eight generals fled one after another. Zhao Yun pressed the advantage, pursuing and striking, while Deng Zhi led the army after him. Zhao Yun penetrated deep into dangerous ground when suddenly tremendous cries rose on every side. Deng Zhi hastily recalled his troops and retreated, but Dong Xi attacked from the left and Xue Ze from the right. Deng Zhi had too few troops and could not rescue him. Zhao Yun was trapped at the heart of the encirclement. He charged east and broke west, but the Wei ranks only grew denser.

p.src: At this time Zhao Yun had only a little over a thousand men. Fighting their way to the foot of a slope, they saw Xiahou Mao directing the entire army from the hilltop. Whenever Zhao Yun turned east, Xiahou Mao pointed east; whenever he turned west, Mao pointed west. Thus Zhao Yun could not break through, so he led his men in an attempt to climb the hill. But logs and stones came crashing down from halfway up, and he could not ascend. Zhao Yun fought from the hour of the dragon until the hour of the cock, yet could find no way out. At last he dismounted to rest briefly and wait for moonlight before fighting again. He had only just removed his armor and sat down. As the moonlight first appeared, flames suddenly soared on every side and the thunder of drums shook the ground. Arrows and stones fell like rain as the Wei troops attacked, all shouting, “Zhao Yun, surrender at once!” Zhao Yun hastily mounted to meet the enemy. Troops closed in from every side, and crossbow bolts shot thickly from all eight directions, so neither men nor horses could advance. Zhao Yun looked up to heaven and sighed, “Because I refused to admit my age, I shall die in this place!”

p.src: Suddenly, tremendous shouting arose from the northeast corner, and the Wei soldiers scattered in confusion. A body of troops came charging in, led by a great general wielding an eighteen-foot tempered-steel spear, with a human head hanging beneath his horse's neck. Zhao Yun looked and saw that it was Zhang Bao. Seeing Zhao Yun, Zhang Bao said, “The Chancellor feared that some mishap might befall you, old General, and therefore specially sent me with five thousand troops to support you. When I heard that you were surrounded, I fought my way through the encirclement. I happened upon the Wei general Xue Ze and slew him.” Zhao Yun was overjoyed and at once fought his way out through the northwest corner with Zhang Bao. They saw the Wei soldiers casting aside their spears and fleeing. Another body of troops charged in from outside with loud battle cries, led by a great general carrying the Green Dragon Crescent Blade and holding a human head in one hand. Zhao Yun looked and saw that it was Guan Xing. Guan Xing said, “By the Chancellor's command, and fearing that some mishap might befall you, old General, I have specially brought five thousand troops to support you. Just now on the battlefield I encountered the Wei general Dong Xi; I cut him down with one stroke, and here is his severed head. The Chancellor will arrive shortly behind me.” Zhao Yun said, “You two generals have already performed extraordinary feats. Why not seize Xiahou Mao today and thereby settle the great affair?”

Pei Xu drew it from next to his skin; it was soaked through with sweat.
He let Cui Liang glance at it, then hurriedly ordered his attendants to give him a fresh horse and rode out of the city toward Tianshui.

p.src: Within two days another mounted messenger arrived, reporting that the Governor of Tianshui had already raised troops and gone to relieve Nan'an, and asking Anding to support him. Cui Liang consulted with the officials of his administration. The officials said, “If we do not go to their aid, Nan'an will be lost and the Imperial Son-in-law Xiahou will be delivered to the enemy; the blame will fall upon both our commanderies. We have no choice but to rescue him.” Cui Liang immediately mustered his troops and left the city, leaving only civil officials behind to guard it. Cui Liang led his army down the main road toward Nan'an. Seeing flames soaring into the sky in the distance, he urged his troops onward through the night. When they were still more than fifty li from Nan'an, tremendous shouting suddenly erupted before and behind them. A scout galloped up and reported, “Guan Xing is blocking the road ahead, and Zhang Bao is attacking from the rear!” The soldiers of Anding fled in every direction. Greatly alarmed, Cui Liang took more than a hundred of his men, fought desperately along a side road until he broke free, and fled back toward Anding. Just as he reached the city moat, a hail of arrows shot down from the walls. From atop the walls, the Shu general Wei Yan called out, “I have already taken the city! Why do you not surrender at once?” It turned out that Wei Yan had disguised his men as soldiers of Anding and tricked the guards into opening the gates late at night, whereupon the Shu troops all poured in; thus Anding had been captured.

p.src: In panic, Cui Liang fled toward Tianshui Commandery. Before he had traveled even one stage, he found a body of troops drawn up ahead. Beneath a great banner sat a man in a silk headscarf, holding a feather fan and wearing a Daoist robe and crane-feather cloak, upright in his carriage. Cui Liang looked and saw that it was Kongming; he hastily wheeled his horse around and fled. The forces of Guan Xing and Zhang Bao came pursuing from two directions, crying only, “Surrender at once!” Seeing Shu soldiers on every side, Cui Liang had no choice but to surrender, and returned with them to the main camp. Kongming treated him as an honored guest. Kongming asked, “Are you on close terms with the Governor of Nan'an?” Cui Liang replied, “That man is Yang Ling, a clansman and younger cousin of Yang Fu. As our commanderies are neighbors, our friendship is very close.” Kongming said, “I would now trouble you to enter the city and persuade Yang Ling to seize Xiahou Mao. Will you do it?” Cui Liang replied, “If the Chancellor commands me to go, you may temporarily withdraw your forces and allow me to enter the city and persuade him.” Kongming accepted his proposal and immediately issued orders for the armies on all four sides to withdraw twenty li and make camp.

p.src: Cui Liang rode alone to the city, called for the gate to be opened, and entered the government offices, where, after exchanging courtesies with Yang Ling, he related the whole affair in detail. Yang Ling said, “We have received great favor from the ruler of Wei. How could we bear to betray him? We should turn their scheme against them.” He then took Cui Liang to Xiahou Mao and explained everything in full. Xiahou Mao asked, “What plan should we use?” Yang Ling replied, “Simply pretend that I am offering up the city gate, lure the Shu troops inside, and then slaughter them within the city.” Cui Liang acted according to the plan. Leaving the city, he met Kongming and said, “Yang Ling will offer up the city gate and admit the main army so that Xiahou Mao may be captured. Yang Ling originally wished to seize him himself, but, having too few brave men under his command, he has not dared to act rashly.” Kongming said, “That is easily done. You now have more than a hundred of your former surrendered soldiers. Conceal Shu generals among them disguised as troops from Anding, take them into the city, and first station them in ambush near Xiahou Mao’s residence. Then secretly arrange with Yang Ling that at midnight he open the city gate, so that those within and without may act together.” Cui Liang thought privately, “If I do not take Shu generals with me, Kongming may grow suspicious. I shall take them inside, behead them there first, and raise a fire as the signal; then we can lure Kongming in and kill him.” He therefore agreed. Kongming instructed him, “I shall send my trusted officers Guan Xing and Zhang Bao ahead with you. Say only that reinforcements have fought their way into the city, so as to reassure Xiahou Mao. As soon as the fire is raised, I shall personally enter the city and capture him.”

p.src: It was dusk. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao received Kongming’s secret instructions, donned their armor, mounted their horses, and took up their weapons. Mingling with the Anding troops, they followed Cui Liang to the walls of Nan’an. From atop the wall, Yang Ling raised the suspended drawboard, leaned against the protective railing, and called, “Whose troops are you?” Cui Liang replied, “Reinforcements from Anding have arrived.” Cui Liang first shot a signal arrow onto the wall. Attached to it was a secret letter saying, “Zhuge Liang has sent two generals ahead to lie concealed within the city, intending to coordinate an attack from inside and out. Do not alarm them, lest the plan be exposed. We shall deal with them after they enter the residence.” Yang Ling showed the letter to Xiahou Mao and explained the matter in detail. Xiahou Mao said, “Since Zhuge Liang has fallen into our trap, have more than a hundred executioners lie in ambush within the residence. When the two generals follow Governor Cui to the residence and dismount, close the gates and behead them. Then raise a fire upon the wall and lure Zhuge Liang into the city. When all our ambushers rush out, Liang can be captured.”

p.src: When all was arranged, Yang Ling returned to the wall and called, “Since these are troops from Anding, they may be admitted into the city.” Guan Xing rode first beside Cui Liang, with Zhang Bao behind. Yang Ling descended from the wall to welcome them beside the gate. Guan Xing raised his blade and brought it down, cutting Yang Ling from his horse. Cui Liang was appalled and hastily wheeled his horse to flee. When he reached the drawbridge, Zhang Bao shouted, “Villain, do not flee! How could your treacherous scheme deceive the Prime Minister?” With one thrust of his spear, he struck Cui Liang from his horse. Guan Xing had already reached the wall and raised the fire signal. Shu troops poured in from every side. Caught utterly unprepared, Xiahou Mao opened the southern gate and fought his way out with all his strength. A body of troops barred his way, led by the general Wang Ping. After a single exchange on horseback, Wang Ping captured Xiahou Mao alive in the saddle, while all the others were slain.

p.src: Kongming entered Nan’an, issued proclamations reassuring the soldiers and people, and allowed not so much as a hair to be harmed. The generals each presented their achievements. Kongming had Xiahou Mao confined in a prison cart. Deng Zhi asked, “Prime Minister, how did you know that Cui Liang was deceiving us?” Kongming replied, “I already knew that fellow had no true intention of surrendering, so I deliberately let him enter the city. He was certain to tell Xiahou Mao everything and try to turn my own scheme against me. From his manner when he returned, I knew well enough that he was false; yet I sent the two generals with him to set his mind at ease. Had he been sincere, he would certainly have tried to prevent it. His eager agreement to take them showed that he feared I might suspect him. He reckoned that once the two generals accompanied him, he could lure them into the city and kill them at his leisure. Their presence would also give our army grounds for confidence and make us advance without concern. But I had already secretly instructed the two generals to act beneath the city gate. There could be no preparations within the city; by sending our army in directly behind them, we struck when the enemy least expected it.” The generals bowed in admiration. Kongming said, “The man who deceived Cui Liang was one of my trusted followers, whom I had pose as the Wei general Pei Xu. I also sent him to deceive Tianshui Commandery, but he has not yet returned, and I do not know why. We can now take advantage of our momentum to seize it.” He therefore left Wu Yi to guard Nan’an and Liu Yan to guard Anding, and freed Wei Yan’s troops to march against Tianshui Commandery.

p.src: Now Ma Zun, Governor of Tianshui Commandery, heard that Xiahou Mao was trapped within the city of Nan’an and assembled his civil and military officers to deliberate. Liang Xu, Officer of Merit; Yin Shang, Registrar; Liang Qian, Secretary; and the others said, “Imperial Son-in-law Xiahou is of the imperial blood. Should any mishap befall him, we could scarcely escape punishment for standing idly by. Why does Your Excellency not muster every soldier under your command and go to his rescue?” As Ma Zun hesitated in doubt, Pei Xu, a trusted man supposedly dispatched by Imperial Son-in-law Xiahou, suddenly arrived. Pei Xu entered the offices, handed an official dispatch to Ma Zun, and said, “The Commander requests troops from both Anding and Tianshui Commanderies to come to his relief with all speed, traveling day and night.” As soon as he had spoken, he hurried away. The next day another courier arrived, reporting, “The Anding troops have already gone on ahead. The Governor is to hurry forward and join them at once.” Just as Ma Zun was about to muster his troops, a man suddenly entered from outside and said, “Your Excellency has fallen into Zhuge Liang’s trap!” All looked at him. He was a native of Ji in Tianshui, surnamed Jiang, given name Wei, and styled Boyue. His father, Jiang Jiong, had once served as Officer of Merit in Tianshui Commandery and had died in the service of the state during a Qiang uprising. From childhood Jiang Wei had read widely in every kind of book and mastered both the arts of war and martial skills. He served his mother with the utmost filial devotion, and the people of the commandery respected him. Later he became a General of the Household and took part in the military affairs of his command.

p.src: That day Jiang Wei said to Ma Zun, “I recently heard that Zhuge Liang defeated Xiahou Mao and has him besieged in Nan’an so tightly that not even water can leak through. How, then, could anyone have escaped from within those encircling ranks? Moreover, Pei Xu is an obscure subordinate officer. We have never seen him before. Furthermore, the messenger from Anding carried no official dispatch. Judging from these facts, that man must be a Shu general falsely claiming to be an officer of Wei. Once he has lured Your Excellency out of the city, he will expect the defenses within to be empty. He has surely concealed a force nearby to seize Tianshui while it lies unguarded.” Ma Zun suddenly understood and said, “But for your words, Boyue, I would have fallen into this treacherous scheme!” Jiang Wei smiled and said, “Set your mind at ease, Your Excellency. I have a plan that can capture Zhuge Liang and relieve the danger at Nan’an.” Indeed:
